claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Oba et al., 2013a.

claims.claim: P. pyralis and A. lateralis represent the two major firefly subfamilies, Lampyrinae and Luciolinae.
claims.source: These two fireflies represent the two major firefly subfamilies, Lampyrinae and Luciolinae, which diverged from a common ancestor over 100 Mya (Figure 1B) (Misof et al., 2014; Mckenna et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as taxonomic fact.

claims.claim: Lampyrinae and Luciolinae diverged from a common ancestor over 100 Mya.
claims.source: These two fireflies represent the two major firefly subfamilies, Lampyrinae and Luciolinae, which diverged from a common ancestor over 100 Mya (Figure 1B) (Misof et al., 2014; Mckenna et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Misof et al., 2014 and Mckenna et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Raphaël Dubois used 'Pyrophorus' to establish the enzymatic basis of bioluminescence in the late 1800s.
claims.source: To facilitate evolutionary comparisons, we also sequenced the 'Cucubano', Ignelater luminosus (Figure 1B), a Caribbean bioluminescent click beetle, and member of the 'Pyrophorus' used by Raphaël Dubois (1849-1929) to first establish the enzymatic basis of bioluminescence in the late 1800s (Dubois, 1885; Dubois, 1886).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Dubois, 1885 and Dubois, 1886.

claims.claim: P. pyralis adult males were collected from the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, USA and Mercer Meadows New Jersey, USA.
claims.source: Photinus pyralis adult males were collected from the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, USA (GSMNP) and Mercer Meadows New Jersey, USA (MMNJ) (Figure 1C), and sequenced using short-insert, mate-pair, Hi-C, and long-read Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) approaches (Appendix 4—table 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the sample collection for the study.

claims.claim: P. pyralis was sequenced using short-insert, mate-pair, Hi-C, and long-read Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) approaches.
claims.source: Photinus pyralis adult males were collected from the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, USA (GSMNP) and Mercer Meadows New Jersey, USA (MMNJ) (Figure 1C), and sequenced using short-insert, mate-pair, Hi-C, and long-read Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) approaches (Appendix 4—table 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the sequencing methods used.

claims.claim: The P. pyralis datasets were combined in a MaSuRCA hybrid genome assembly.
claims.source: These datasets were combined in a MaSuRCA (Zimin et al., 2013) hybrid genome assembly (Appendix 1.5).
claims.evidence: This describes the assembly method used.

claims.claim: The A. lateralis genome was derived from an ALL-PATHs assembly of short insert and mate-pair reads from a single adult female.
claims.source: The Aquatica lateralis genome was derived from an ALL-PATHs (Butler et al., 2008) assembly of short insert and mate-pair reads from a single adult female from a laboratory-reared population, whose lineage, dubbed 'Ikeya-Y90', was first collected 25 years ago from a now extinct population in Yokohama, Japan (Appendix 2.5).
claims.evidence: This describes the assembly method and sample source.

claims.claim: The A. lateralis 'Ikeya-Y90' lineage was first collected 25 years ago from a now extinct population in Yokohama, Japan.
claims.source: The Aquatica lateralis genome was derived from an ALL-PATHs (Butler et al., 2008) assembly of short insert and mate-pair reads from a single adult female from a laboratory-reared population, whose lineage, dubbed 'Ikeya-Y90', was first collected 25 years ago from a now extinct population in Yokohama, Japan (Appendix 2.5).
claims.evidence: This provides historical information about the sample lineage.

claims.claim: A single I. luminosus adult male collected in Mayagüez Puerto Rico, USA, was used to produce a high-coverage Supernova linked-read draft genome.
claims.source: A single Ignelater luminosus adult male, collected in Mayagüez Puerto Rico, USA, was used to produce a high-coverage Supernova (Weisenfeld et al., 2017) linked-read draft genome (Appendix 3.5), which was further manually scaffolded using low-coverage long-read Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing (Appendix 3.5.4).
claims.evidence: This describes the sample and assembly method.

claims.claim: The I. luminosus genome was further manually scaffolded using low-coverage long-read Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing.
claims.source: A single Ignelater luminosus adult male, collected in Mayagüez Puerto Rico, USA, was used to produce a high-coverage Supernova (Weisenfeld et al., 2017) linked-read draft genome (Appendix 3.5), which was further manually scaffolded using low-coverage long-read Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing (Appendix 3.5.4).
claims.evidence: This describes additional assembly refinement.

claims.claim: The gene completeness and contiguity statistics of P. pyralis (Ppyr1.3) and A. lateralis (Alat1.3) genome assemblies are comparable to the genome of the model beetle Tribolium castaneum.
claims.source: The gene completeness and contiguity statistics of our P. pyralis (Ppyr1.3) and A. lateralis (Alat1.3) genome assemblies are comparable to the genome of the model beetle Tribolium castaneum (Figure 2F; Appendix 4.1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The I. luminosus genome assembly (Ilumi1.2) is less complete than P. pyralis and A. lateralis, but is comparable to other published insect genomes.
claims.source: The I. luminosus genome assembly (Ilumi1.2) is less complete, but is comparable to other published insect genomes (Figure 2F; Appendix 4.1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus coding gene annotation sets contain 94.2%, 90.0%, and 91.8% of the Endopterygota BUSCOs, respectively.
claims.source: These coding gene annotation sets for P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus are comprised of 15,773, 14,285, and 27,557 genes containing 94.2%, 90.0%, and 91.8% of the Endopterygota Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCOs) (Simão et al., 2015), respectively.
claims.evidence: This provides quantitative assessment of annotation completeness using BUSCO analysis.

claims.claim: 77% of genes were found in orthogroups with at least one other species.
claims.source: Protein clustering via predicted orthology indicated 77% of genes were found in orthogroups with at least one other species (Figure 2E; Appendix 4—figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on orthology analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The greatest orthogroup overlap was found between the P. pyralis and A. lateralis genesets.
claims.source: We found the greatest orthogroup overlap between the P. pyralis and A. lateralis genesets, as expected given the more recent phylogenetic divergence of these species.
claims.evidence: This is based on orthology analysis and is consistent with phylogenetic expectations.

claims.claim: Remaining redundancy in the P. pyralis assembly is likely due to the heterozygosity of the outbred input libraries.
claims.source: Remaining redundancy in the P. pyralis assembly and annotation, as indicated by duplicates of the BUSCOs and the assembly size (Figure 2F; Appendix 4—table 2) is likely due to the heterozygosity of the outbred input libraries (Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on assembly characteristics and knowledge of the sample source.

claims.claim: The P. pyralis genome assembly was super-scaffolded into 11 pseudo-chromosomal linkage groups using Hi-C proximity-ligation linkage approach.
claims.source: To enable the characterization of long-range genetic structure, we super-scaffolded the P. pyralis genome assembly into 11 pseudo-chromosomal linkage groups using a Hi-C proximity-ligation linkage approach (Figure 2A; Appendix 1.5.3).
claims.evidence: This describes the scaffolding method and is shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The 11 P. pyralis linkage groups contain 95% of the assembly (448.8 Mbp).
claims.source: These linkage groups contain 95% of the assembly (448.8 Mbp).
claims.evidence: This provides quantitative information about the scaffolding results.

claims.claim: Linkage group LG3a corresponds to the X-chromosome based on expected adult XO male read coverage and gene content.
claims.source: Linkage group LG3a corresponds to the X-chromosome based on expected adult XO male read coverage and gene content (Appendix 1.6.4.1) and its size (22.2 Mbp) is comparable to the expected X-chromosome size based on sex-specific genome size estimates using flow cytometry (~26 Mbp) (Lower et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on coverage analysis and gene content analysis.

claims.claim: The P. pyralis X-chromosome size (22.2 Mbp) is comparable to the expected X-chromosome size based on sex-specific genome size estimates using flow cytometry (~26 Mbp).
claims.source: Linkage group LG3a corresponds to the X-chromosome based on expected adult XO male read coverage and gene content (Appendix 1.6.4.1) and its size (22.2 Mbp) is comparable to the expected X-chromosome size based on sex-specific genome size estimates using flow cytometry (~26 Mbp) (Lower et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Lower et al., 2017 and comparison of assembly data to flow cytometry estimates.

claims.claim: Homologs to T. castaneum X-chromosome genes were enriched on LG3a over every other linkage group.
claims.source: Homologs to T. castaneum X-chromosome genes were enriched on LG3a over every other linkage group, suggesting that the X-chromosomes of these distantly related beetles are homologous, and that their content has been reasonably conserved for >200 MY (Appendix 1.6.4.1) (Mckenna et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claims.claim: The X-chromosomes of P. pyralis and T. castaneum are homologous, and their content has been reasonably conserved for >200 MY.
claims.source: Homologs to T. castaneum X-chromosome genes were enriched on LG3a over every other linkage group, suggesting that the X-chromosomes of these distantly related beetles are homologous, and that their content has been reasonably conserved for >200 MY (Appendix 1.6.4.1) (Mckenna et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on gene content analysis and supported by phylogenetic dating from Mckenna et al., 2015.

claims.claim: P. pyralis Luc1 and LST are located on separate linkage groups.
claims.source: We hypothesized that the P. pyralis orthologs of known bioluminescence genes, including the canonical luciferase Luc1 (de Wet et al., 1985) and the specialized luciferin sulfotransferase LST (Fallon et al., 2016), would be located on the same linkage group to facilitate chromosomal looping and enhancer assisted co-expression within the light organ. We, however, found these genes on separate linkage groups (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and contradicts the initial hypothesis.

claims.claim: The complete mitochondrial genomes of P. pyralis and I. luminosus were assembled.
claims.source: In addition to nuclear genome assembly and coding gene annotation, we also assembled the complete mitochondrial genomes (mtDNA) of P. pyralis (Figure 2C; Appendix 1.8) and I. luminosus (Appendix 3.10), while the mtDNA sequence of A. lateralis was recently published (Maeda et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the mitochondrial genome assembly work.

claims.claim: The mtDNA sequence of A. lateralis was recently published.
claims.source: In addition to nuclear genome assembly and coding gene annotation, we also assembled the complete mitochondrial genomes (mtDNA) of P. pyralis (Figure 2C; Appendix 1.8) and I. luminosus (Appendix 3.10), while the mtDNA sequence of A. lateralis was recently published (Maeda et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Maeda et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The mtDNA assemblies show high conservation of gene content and synteny, with the exception of the variable ~1 Kbp tandem repeat unit (TRU) found in the firefly mtDNAs.
claims.source: These mtDNA assemblies show high conservation of gene content and synteny, with the exception of the variable ~1 Kbp tandem repeat unit (TRU) found in the firefly mtDNAs.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of the assembled mitochondrial genomes.

claims.claim: 42.6%, 19.8%, and 34.1% of the P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus assemblies were found to be repetitive, respectively.
claims.source: Overall, 42.6%, 19.8%, and 34.1% of the P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus assemblies were found to be repetitive, respectively (Appendix 1.11; 2.9; 3.9).
claims.evidence: This provides quantitative data on repeat content.

claims.claim: 66.7%, 39.4%, and 55% of repeats in P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus could not be classified as any known repetitive sequence, respectively.
claims.source: Of these repeats 66.7%, 39.4%, and 55% could not be classified as any known repetitive sequence, respectively.
claims.evidence: This provides quantitative data on unclassified repeat content.

claims.claim: Helitrons are among the most abundant individual repeat elements in the P. pyralis assembly.
claims.source: Helitrons, DNA transposons that transpose through rolling circle replication (Kapitonov and Jurka, 2001), are among the most abundant individual repeat elements in the P. pyralis assembly.
claims.evidence: This is based on repeat annotation analysis.

claims.claim: P. pyralis chromosomes have canonical telomeres with telomeric repeats (TTAGG).
claims.source: Via in situ hybridization, we identified that P. pyralis chromosomes have canonical telomeres with telomeric repeats (TTAGG) (Figure 2B; Appendix 1.13).
claims.evidence: This is shown by FISH data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Methylation at CpGs (mCG) was unambiguously detected at ~20% within the genic regions of P. pyralis.
claims.source: Methylation at CpGs (mCG) was unambiguously detected at ~20% within the genic regions of P. pyralis and its methylation levels were at least twice those reported from other holometabolous insects (Figure 2D; Appendix 1.12).
claims.evidence: This is based on whole genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: P. pyralis methylation levels were at least twice those reported from other holometabolous insects.
claims.source: Methylation at CpGs (mCG) was unambiguously detected at ~20% within the genic regions of P. pyralis and its methylation levels were at least twice those reported from other holometabolous insects (Figure 2D; Appendix 1.12).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of WGBS data to published data, shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Direct orthologs of both DNMT1 and DNMT3 were conserved in P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus.
claims.source: Molecular evolution analyses of the DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) show that direct orthologs of both DNMT1 and DNMT3 were conserved in P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus (Appendix 4—figure 2; Appendix 4.2.3), implying that our three study species, and inferentially likely most firefly lineages, possess mCG.
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of DNMT genes.

claims.claim: The three study species, and inferentially likely most firefly lineages, possess mCG.
claims.source: Molecular evolution analyses of the DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) show that direct orthologs of both DNMT1 and DNMT3 were conserved in P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus (Appendix 4—figure 2; Appendix 4.2.3), implying that our three study species, and inferentially likely most firefly lineages, possess mCG.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of DNMT genes and CpG[O/E] analysis.

claims.claim: Two luciferase paralogs have been previously described in fireflies.
claims.source: Two luciferase paralogs have been previously described in fireflies (Oba et al., 2013a; Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Oba et al., 2013a and Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017.

claims.claim: P. pyralis Luc1 was the first firefly luciferase cloned.
claims.source: P. pyralis Luc1 was the first firefly luciferase cloned (de Wet et al., 1985), and its direct orthologs have been widely identified from other fireflies (Oba, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to de Wet et al., 1985.

claims.claim: Direct orthologs of P. pyralis Luc1 have been widely identified from other fireflies.
claims.source: P. pyralis Luc1 was the first firefly luciferase cloned (de Wet et al., 1985), and its direct orthologs have been widely identified from other fireflies (Oba, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Oba, 2014.

claims.claim: Luc2 was previously known only from a handful of Asian taxa, including A. lateralis.
claims.source: The luciferase paralog Luc2 was previously known only from a handful of Asian taxa, including A. lateralis (Oba et al., 2013a; Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Oba et al., 2013a and Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In Asian taxa, Luc1 is responsible for light production from the lanterns of adults, larvae, prepupae and pupae.
claims.source: Previous investigations of these Asian taxa have shown that Luc1 is responsible for light production from the lanterns of adults, larvae, prepupae and pupae, whereas Luc2 is responsible for the dim glow of eggs, ovaries, prepupae and the whole pupal body (Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In Asian taxa, Luc2 is responsible for the dim glow of eggs, ovaries, prepupae and the whole pupal body.
claims.source: Previous investigations of these Asian taxa have shown that Luc1 is responsible for light production from the lanterns of adults, larvae, prepupae and pupae, whereas Luc2 is responsible for the dim glow of eggs, ovaries, prepupae and the whole pupal body (Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Two firefly luciferases, Luc1 and Luc2, were unequivocally identified in both the P. pyralis and A. lateralis genomes.
claims.source: From our curated genesets (Appendix 1.10; 2.8), we unequivocally identified two firefly luciferases, Luc1 and Luc2, in both the P. pyralis and A. lateralis genomes.
claims.evidence: This is based on gene annotation and curation.

claims.claim: In both P. pyralis and A. lateralis, Luc1 is the sole luciferase expressed in the lanterns of both larvae and adults, regardless of sex.
claims.source: Our RNA-Seq data further show that in both P. pyralis and A. lateralis, Luc1 and Luc2 display expression patterns consistent with previous reports. While Luc1 is the sole luciferase expressed in the lanterns of both larvae and adults, regardless of sex, Luc2 is expressed in other tissues and stages, such as eggs (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: In both P. pyralis and A. lateralis, Luc2 is expressed in other tissues and stages, such as eggs.
claims.source: Our RNA-Seq data further show that in both P. pyralis and A. lateralis, Luc1 and Luc2 display expression patterns consistent with previous reports. While Luc1 is the sole luciferase expressed in the lanterns of both larvae and adults, regardless of sex, Luc2 is expressed in other tissues and stages, such as eggs (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Luc2 expression is detected in RNA libraries derived from adult female bodies (without head or lantern), suggesting detection of ovary expression.
claims.source: Notably, Luc2 expression is detected in RNA libraries derived from adult female bodies (without head or lantern), suggesting detection of ovary expression as described in previous studies (Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data and is consistent with previous reports cited.

claims.claim: Since their divergence via gene duplication prior to the divergence of Lampyrinae and Luciolinae, Luc1 and Luc2 have established different, but conserved roles in bioluminescence throughout the firefly life cycle.
claims.source: Together, these results support that since their divergence via gene duplication prior to the divergence of Lampyrinae and Luciolinae, Luc1 and Luc2 have established different, but conserved roles in bioluminescence throughout the firefly life cycle.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on expression data and phylogenetic relationships.

claims.claim: Firefly luciferase is hypothesized to be derived from an ancestral peroxisomal fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (PACS).
claims.source: Firefly luciferase is hypothesized to be derived from an ancestral peroxisomal fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (PACS) (Figure 3A) (Oba et al., 2003; Oba et al., 2006a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Oba et al., 2003 and Oba et al., 2006a.

claims.claim: In both firefly species, Luc1 is genomically clustered with its closely related homologs, including PACSs and non-peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSs).
claims.source: We found that, in both firefly species, Luc1 is genomically clustered with its closely related homologs, including PACSs and non-peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSs), enzymes which can be distinguished by the presence/absence of a C-terminal peroxisomal-targeting-signal-1 (PTS1).
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic synteny analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Microsomal glutathione S-transferase (MGST) family genes were found nearby Luc1 and are directly orthologous between both firefly species.
claims.source: We also found nearby microsomal glutathione S-transferase (MGST) family genes (Figure 3D) that are directly orthologous between both species,
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic synteny analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Luc1 and Luc2 are highly conserved at the level of gene structure—both are composed of seven exons with completely conserved exon/intron boundaries.
claims.source: Luc1 and Luc2 are highly conserved at the level of gene structure—both are composed of seven exons with completely conserved exon/intron boundaries (Appendix 4—figure 4; Appendix 4—figure 5), and most members of Clades A, B, and C also have seven exons.
claims.evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis.

claims.claim: Most members of Clades A, B, and C also have seven exons.
claims.source: Luc1 and Luc2 are highly conserved at the level of gene structure—both are composed of seven exons with completely conserved exon/intron boundaries (Appendix 4—figure 4; Appendix 4—figure 5), and most members of Clades A, B, and C also have seven exons.
claims.evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis.

claims.claim: Luc2 is located on a different linkage-group from Luc1 in P. pyralis and on a different scaffold from Luc1 in A. lateralis.
claims.source: Luc2 is located on a different linkage-group from Luc1 in P. pyralis and on a different scaffold from Luc1 in A. lateralis, consistent with the interpretation that Luc1 and Luc2 lie on different chromosomes in both firefly species.
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic location data.

claims.claim: No PACS or ACS genes were found in the vicinity of Luc2 in either firefly species.
claims.source: No PACS or ACS genes were found in the vicinity of Luc2 in either species.
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic synteny analysis.

claims.claim: Tandem gene duplication in a firefly ancestor gave rise to several ancestral PACS paralogs, one of which neofunctionalized in place to become the ancestral luciferase (AncLuc).
claims.source: These data support that tandem gene duplication in a firefly ancestor gave rise to several ancestral PACS paralogs, one of which neofunctionalized in place to become the ancestral luciferase (AncLuc) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is an evolutionary model inferred from synteny and phylogenetic data, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Prior to the divergence of the firefly subfamilies Lampyrinae and Luciolinae around 100 Mya, AncLuc duplicated, possibly via a long-range gene duplication event, and then subfunctionalized to give rise to Luc2, while the original AncLuc subfunctionalized in place to give rise to Luc1.
claims.source: Prior to the divergence of the firefly subfamilies Lampyrinae and Luciolinae around 100 Mya (Appendix 4.3), this AncLuc duplicated, possibly via a long-range gene duplication event (e.g. transposon mobilization), and then subfunctionalized in its transcript expression pattern to give rise to Luc2, while the original AncLuc subfunctionalized in place to give rise to Luc1 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is an evolutionary model inferred from synteny, phylogenetic, and expression data, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: A single luciferase was identified in the I. luminosus genome which was highly expressed in both the dorsal prothorax and ventral abdominal lanterns.
claims.source: Unlike some other described bioluminescent Elateridae, which have separate luciferases expressed in the dorsal prothorax and ventral abdominal lanterns (Oba et al., 2010a), we identified only a single luciferase in the I. luminosus genome which was highly expressed in both of the lanterns (Figure 3C; Appendix 3.8).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene annotation and RNA-Seq expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The exon number and exon-intron splice junctions of IlumLuc are identical to those of firefly luciferases.
claims.source: The exon number and exon-intron splice junctions of IlumLuc are identical to those of firefly luciferases, but unlike the firefly luciferases which have short introns less than <100 bp long, IlumLuc has two long introns (Appendix 4—figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis.

claims.claim: IlumLuc has two long introns, unlike firefly luciferases which have short introns less than 100 bp long.
claims.source: The exon number and exon-intron splice junctions of IlumLuc are identical to those of firefly luciferases, but unlike the firefly luciferases which have short introns less than <100 bp long, IlumLuc has two long introns (Appendix 4—figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis.

claims.claim: Several PACS genes in the I. luminosus genome were related to IlumLuc and formed a clade (Clade D) specific to the Elateridae.
claims.source: We found several PACS genes in the I. luminosus genome which were related to IlumLuc and formed a clade (Clade D) specific to the Elateridae (Figure 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The IlumLuc locus is not orthologous to the extant firefly Luc1 locus.
claims.source: We infer that the IlumLuc locus is not orthologous to the extant firefly Luc1 locus, as IlumLuc is not physically clustered with Clade A, B or C ACS or PACS genes (Figure 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on synteny analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: A different scaffold in I. luminosus (Scaffold 9654) is likely orthologous to the firefly Luc1 locus.
claims.source: We instead identified a different scaffold in I. luminosus that is likely orthologous to the firefly Luc1 locus (Scaffold 9654; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on synteny analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The genomic structures are consistent with independent origins of firefly and click beetle luciferases.
claims.source: Overall, these genomic structures are consistent with independent origins of firefly and click beetle luciferases.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on synteny analysis.

claims.claim: Ancestral state reconstruction recovers at least two gains of luciferase activity in bioluminescent beetles.
claims.source: We then carried out targeted molecular evolution analyses including the known beetle luciferases and their closely related homologs. Ancestral state reconstruction of luminescent activity on the gene tree using Mesquite (Maddison and Maddison, 2017) recovered two independent gains of luminescence as the most parsimonious and likely scenario: once in click beetles, and once in the common ancestor of firefly, phengodid, and rhagophthalmid beetles (Figure 4A; Appendix 4.3.3).
claims.evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: 35% of the sites of the branch leading to the ancestral click beetle luciferase showed a statistically significant signal of episodic positive selection with dN/dS > 1 (ω or max dN/dS = 3.98).
claims.source: In an independent molecular adaptation analysis utilizing the coding nucleotide sequence of the elaterid luciferases and their close homologs within Elateridae, 35% of the sites of the branch leading to the ancestral click beetle luciferase showed a statistically significant signal of episodic positive selection with dN/dS > 1 (ω or max dN/dS = 3.98) as compared to the evolution of its paralogs using the aBSREL branch-site selection test (Smith et al., 2015) (Figure 4B; Appendix 4.3.4).
claims.evidence: This is based on molecular adaptation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The common ancestor of the click beetle luciferases (EAncLuc) underwent a period of accelerated directional evolution.
claims.source: This implies that the common ancestor of the click beetle luciferases (EAncLuc) underwent a period of accelerated directional evolution.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the positive selection signal detected.

claims.claim: The identified selection signal represents the relatively recent neofunctionalization of click beetle luciferase from a non-luminous ancestral Clade D PACS gene.
claims.source: As the branch under selection in the molecular adaptation analysis (Figure 4B) is the same branch of luciferase activity gain via ancestral reconstruction (Figure 4A), we conclude that the identified selection signal represents the relatively recent neofunctionalization of click beetle luciferase from a non-luminous ancestral Clade D PACS gene, distinct from the more ancient neofunctionalization of firefly luciferase.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on integration of ancestral state reconstruction and molecular adaptation analyses.

claims.claim: The neofunctionalization of EAncLuc occurred after the divergence of the elaterid subfamily Agrypninae.
claims.source: Based on the constraints from our tree, we determine that this neofunctionalization of EAncLuc occured after the divergence of the elaterid subfamily Agrypninae.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic constraints.

claims.claim: There is evidence for a subsequent luciferase duplication event in phengodids, but not in rhagophthalmids, that is independent of the duplication event that gave rise to Luc1 and Luc2 in fireflies.
claims.source: There is evidence for a subsequent luciferase duplication event in phengodids, but not in rhagophthalmids, that is independent of the duplication event that gave rise to Luc1 and Luc2 in fireflies (Figures 3C and 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figures 3C and 4.

claims.claim: The results strongly support the independent neofunctionalization of luciferase activity in click beetles and fireflies.
claims.source: Altogether, our results strongly support the independent neofunctionalization of luciferase activity in click beetles and fireflies, and therefore at least two independent gains of luciferin-utilizing luminescence in beetles.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claims.claim: There were at least two independent gains of luciferin-utilizing luminescence in beetles.

results.result: High-quality genome assemblies were generated for three bioluminescent beetle species (P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus) using diverse sequencing technologies and assembly approaches. The assemblies show comparable completeness to model beetle genomes, with detailed characterization of genomic features including linkage groups, mitochondrial genomes, repeat content, and telomeric sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C54 collectively describe comprehensive genome sequencing and assembly efforts with appropriate quality metrics (BUSCO scores, N50 values, orthology analysis). The methods are well-documented with multiple sequencing technologies, and quality assessments demonstrate assemblies comparable to established reference genomes. The data presented in Figure 2 supports the assembly quality claims.

results.result: P. pyralis exhibits unusually high DNA methylation levels (~20% mCG in genic regions), at least twice that of other holometabolous insects, with conserved DNA methyltransferases (DNMT1 and DNMT3) present across all three study species.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data (Figure 2D) showing quantitative methylation levels, phylogenetic analysis confirming DNMT conservation, and comparative analysis with published insect methylation data. The inference that most firefly lineages possess mCG is reasonable given the conservation of DNMTs and CpG[O/E] patterns.

results.result: The P. pyralis X-chromosome (LG3a, 22.2 Mbp) was identified through coverage analysis and gene content, showing homology with the T. castaneum X-chromosome with conservation over >200 million years.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: XO male coverage patterns, enrichment of T. castaneum X-chromosome homologs on LG3a, and concordance between assembly size (22.2 Mbp) and flow cytometry estimates (~26 Mbp). The inference of long-term conservation is supported by phylogenetic dating and comparative genomic analysis.

results.result: P. pyralis bioluminescence genes Luc1 and LST are located on separate linkage groups, contrary to the hypothesis that they would be co-localized for coordinated expression.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 is directly supported by genomic mapping data shown in Figure 2A. This finding contradicts the authors' initial hypothesis but is clearly demonstrated by the Hi-C scaffolding results.

results.result: Two luciferase paralogs (Luc1 and Luc2) were identified in both firefly species with distinct, conserved expression patterns: Luc1 is exclusively expressed in adult and larval lanterns, while Luc2 is expressed in eggs, ovaries, and other non-lantern tissues, suggesting subfunctionalization following gene duplication prior to the Lampyrinae-Luciolinae divergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C69 are well-supported by RNA-Seq expression data (Figure 3C), gene annotation, and consistency with previously published studies. The expression patterns are clearly demonstrated across multiple tissues and life stages in both species, supporting the evolutionary model of subfunctionalization.

results.result: Firefly luciferases evolved from ancestral peroxisomal fatty acyl-CoA synthetases (PACS) through tandem gene duplication and neofunctionalization. Luc1 is genomically clustered with related PACS/ACS genes and MGST genes in both firefly species. Prior to the Lampyrinae-Luciolinae split (~100 Mya), the ancestral luciferase (AncLuc) duplicated via long-range duplication, with subsequent subfunctionalization producing Luc1 (in place) and Luc2 (relocated).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C78 are supported by genomic synteny analysis (Figure 3D), phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3C), gene structure conservation, and expression data. The evolutionary model is well-reasoned based on genomic location, orthology relationships, and temporal constraints from phylogenetic dating. The synteny patterns clearly show clustering of related genes at the Luc1 locus but not at Luc2.

results.result: A single luciferase (IlumLuc) was identified in I. luminosus with identical exon structure to firefly luciferases but longer introns. IlumLuc belongs to an Elateridae-specific clade (Clade D) and is not orthologous to the firefly Luc1 locus, with a different I. luminosus scaffold (9654) showing orthology to the firefly Luc1 locus, supporting independent origins of firefly and click beetle luciferases.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C85 are supported by gene annotation, RNA-Seq expression data (Figure 3C), gene structure analysis, phylogenetic analysis, and detailed synteny analysis (Figure 3D). The lack of orthology between IlumLuc and firefly Luc1 loci is demonstrated through absence of conserved syntenic relationships with Clade A/B/C genes, while a different scaffold shows the expected orthologous relationships.

results.result: Multiple independent lines of evidence support at least two independent gains of bioluminescence in beetles: ancestral state reconstruction identifies separate origins in click beetles and in the common ancestor of fireflies/phengodids/rhagophthalmids; molecular adaptation analysis shows 35% of sites in the ancestral click beetle luciferase branch under positive selection (dN/dS = 3.98), indicating neofunctionalization from a non-luminous Clade D PACS gene after Agrypninae divergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C93 are strongly supported by convergent evidence from ancestral state reconstruction (Figure 4A), molecular adaptation analysis using aBSREL (Figure 4B), synteny analysis, and phylogenetic constraints. The positive selection signal on the same branch as luciferase activity gain provides compelling evidence for neofunctionalization. The integration of multiple analytical approaches strengthens the conclusion of independent origins.

results.result: Comparative transcriptomic analysis identified conserved lantern-enriched enzymes in both firefly species, including luciferase, LST (absent in I. luminosus), adenylate kinase, cystathionine gamma-lyase, and ASKSA with peroxisomal targeting signals. The conservation of expression patterns suggests the enzymatic physiology of photocytes was established in the Lampyrinae-Luciolinae ancestor.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C107 are supported by RNA-Seq differential expression analysis (Figure 5) and orthology analysis. The identification of LST in both fireflies but not I. luminosus supports independent evolution. The functional inferences about enzyme roles (C99, C100, C102, C104) are reasonable based on known biochemistry and enrichment patterns, though some represent speculation (C105) about regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: Expression analysis of non-enzyme genes identified lysosomal genes enriched in firefly lanterns, suggesting 'differentiated zone granules' may be lysosomes. An opsin (Rh7) was found highly expressed in A. lateralis but not P. pyralis lanterns, suggesting potential light perception function.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are based on expression data but represent speculative interpretations. The lysosomal hypothesis (C108) lacks direct experimental validation of organelle identity. The Rh7 light perception hypothesis (C110) is based on analogy to Drosophila but requires functional validation. These are reasonable hypotheses requiring follow-up work.

results.result: Lucibufagins were detected in P. pyralis adults and larvae but absent from A. lateralis and I. luminosus, rejecting lucibufagins as ancestral firefly defense compounds and suggesting they are a derived trait of Lampyrinae subfamily.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C122 are supported by LC-HRAM-MS data (Figure 6B) showing clear presence/absence patterns across species and life stages. The inference that lucibufagins are Lampyrinae-specific (C121-C122) is supported by the data and literature (C119), though the alternative hypothesis of loss in A. lateralis (C118) cannot be definitively excluded without broader taxonomic sampling.

results.result: P. pyralis shows a unique expansion of the CYP303 cytochrome P450 family (11 genes plus 2 pseudogenes) via tandem duplication, while 94/97 other insect genomes and both A. lateralis and I. luminosus contain only a single CYP303 gene. This expansion is proposed as a candidate for lucibufagin biosynthesis, though alternative roles in pheromone production are possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 are well-supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 6C), comparative genomics with OrthoDB, and genomic location data (Figure 6D). The correlation with lucibufagin presence is compelling, though the proposed biosynthetic role (C131) remains speculative without functional validation. The authors appropriately acknowledge alternative hypotheses (C132).

results.result: Metagenomic analysis revealed diverse symbionts including the first complete Entomoplasma genome (E. luminosus subsp. pyralis, 1.29 Mbp) prevalent in P. pyralis, Tenericutes sequences in A. lateralis suggesting mollicute symbionts, Proteobacterial sequences in A. lateralis, and limited symbionts in I. luminosus.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C146 are supported by metagenomic assembly, taxonomic annotation, and read coverage analysis. The E. luminosus genome assembly is well-documented (C138-C140). The inferences about symbiont presence in A. lateralis (C143) and absence in I. luminosus (C146) are reasonable based on sequence abundance and coverage patterns, though functional roles remain speculative.

results.result: Two novel orthomyxoviridae-like ssRNA viruses (PpyrOMLV1/2) were discovered in P. pyralis showing high prevalence, multi-generational transovarial transmission, and endogenous viral elements (EVEs), representing the first firefly viruses, second report of Orthomyxoviridae transgenerational transfer, and second report of Orthomyxoviridae EVEs.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C153 are supported by RNA-Seq data analysis, laboratory transmission observations, and genomic EVE identification. The novelty claims (C151-C153) are appropriately supported by citations to prior work establishing the rarity of these findings.

results.result: Background and context claims about firefly biology, bioluminescence biochemistry, taxonomic diversity, prior research, and related beetle families, establishing the scientific foundation and motivation for the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C27 and related background claims are appropriately supported by citations to established literature and represent accurate summaries of prior knowledge. These provide essential context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: The study design involved sequencing two firefly species (P. pyralis and A. lateralis) that diverged over 100 million years ago and a click beetle (I. luminosus) with near-identical bioluminescent biochemistry but anatomically distinct light organs, with analyses supporting independent gains of bioluminescence.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 and C17-C20 accurately describe the study design rationale and anatomical observations (Figure 1B). The divergence time (C3) is supported by phylogenetic dating. The main conclusion (C6) is supported by the comprehensive analyses described in other result groups.

results.result: Discussion of broader evolutionary implications: the independent origins provide a model system for studying parallel enzyme evolution; gene duplication at luciferase loci suggests promiscuous enzymatic activities as raw material for adaptation; specialized bioluminescence subtraits likely arose after luciferase specialization; luciferin may have predated luciferase neofunctionalization; early firefly bioluminescence may have evolved as an aposematic response to predators.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C163 represent interpretive discussion and speculation about evolutionary processes. While C156 is reasonably supported by observed gene duplication patterns, claims about evolutionary sequence (C157), ancestral luciferin presence (C158), symbiont contributions (C159), and early bioluminescence function (C163) are speculative hypotheses requiring additional evidence.
